1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 37-year-old female teacher who was admitted to our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "multiple nodules in both lungs found on physical examination for more than half a year, cough for 1 month." During a physical examination at a local hospital on Day -194, chest CT showed multiple nodules in both lungs (maximum diameter 0.8 cm), of undetermined nature; small mediastinal lymph nodes; and a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs. She had no cough or sputum production, no chest tightness or shortness of breath, and received no treatment. On Day -183, the patient presented to a tertiary hospital in Shanghai, where bronchoscopy showed no neoplasm. Bronchoalveolar lavage was performed in the medial segment of the right middle lobe, and BALF sent for high-throughput sequencing returned Acinetobacter, Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas, Corynebacterium xerosis, Enterococcus faecalis, and Alcaligenes faecalis. TBLB and brushings were performed in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe; pathology and exfoliative cytology indicated chronic inflammatory changes, with no malignant tumor cells seen, and no treatment was given. In approximately 5 months before Day 0, the patient purchased and took Chinese herbal medicine on her own (details unknown) for a total of more than 1 month. On Day -117, repeat chest CT at a local hospital showed multiple nodules in both lungs, somewhat absorbed compared with Day -194; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes; a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs; splenomegaly; and a dense shadow in the liver. During this period, she had no discomfort and received no treatment. On Day -73, repeat chest CT at the local hospital again showed multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs, with lesions similar to those on Day -117; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes. In approximately 1 month before Day 0, after one episode of catching a cold, the patient developed cough and sputum production; the sputum was yellow-white, relatively copious, and easy to expectorate. She had no chest tightness or shortness of breath, and no dizziness or headache. Chest CT performed at the local hospital from Day -6 showed multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs, with increased number and size of lesions compared with Day -73; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes; and a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs. The local hospital recommended that the patient go to a higher-level hospital for further diagnosis and treatment. On Day -4, the patient presented to our hospital, where noncontrast and contrast-enhanced 3D chest CT showed multiple nodules in both lungs, with the dominant lesions located in the lateral basal segment of the right lower lobe and the anterior basal segment of the left lower lobe; mediastinal lymphadenopathy; hepatic calcification; right renal calculus; and splenomegaly. For further diagnosis and treatment, she was admitted from the outpatient clinic with "pulmonary nodules." Since the onset of illness, the patient had been in good general condition, with no significant change in weight, normal appetite, normal bowel and bladder function, and no sleep abnormalities. Further history revealed that the patient had herpes zoster infection in approximately 3 months before Day 0; symptoms improved after standard intravenous medication and topical treatment at an outside hospital (details unknown). At present, multiple postherpetic scars are visible on the right anterior chest wall, flexor aspect of the right arm, and right shoulder/back area (approximately 2*2 cm in length, raised above the skin surface, without tenderness). She denied a history of hypertension, diabetes, or coronary heart disease; denied a history of TB, hepatitis, or other infectious diseases; denied a history of trauma, surgery, or blood transfusion; and reported contrast agent allergy. The patient had long resided in her place of origin and denied a history of contact with contaminated water; had no smoking history; had no alcohol use history; and vaccination history was according to the local schedule. She was married, and her spouse was healthy. Obstetric history: 2-0-0-2; both children are healthy. Family history: parents and younger sister are all healthy; she denied a family history of hereditary disease. Physical examination on admission: temperature 36.2℃, pulse 72/min, respirations 18/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg. The patient was in fair general condition, conscious, with fair mental status and stable vital signs. No enlarged superficial lymph nodes were palpable. Multiple postherpetic scars were visible on the right anterior chest wall, flexor aspect of the right arm, and right shoulder/back area (approximately 2*2 cm in length, raised above the skin surface, without tenderness). Breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales. The spleen was palpable below the costal margin and was soft. No other abnormalities were found in the heart, abdomen, or nervous system, and there was no edema in either lower extremity. The patient's laboratory and ancillary examinations at outside hospitals in 2020 were as follows: On Day +171, chest CT showed multiple nodules in both lungs (maximum diameter 0.8 cm), of undetermined nature; small mediastinal lymph nodes; and a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs. On Day +180, CBC at a tertiary hospital in Shanghai showed: WBC 4.47×10^9/L, neutrophils% 67.1%, lymphocytes% 19.3%↓, monocytes% 11.0%↑, eosinophils% 2.3%, basophils% 0.3%, neutrophils 2.7×10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.8×10^9/L↓, monocytes 0.44×10^9/L, eosinophils 0.09×10^9/L, basophils 0.01×10^9/L, RBC 4.47×10^12/L, hemoglobin 128 g/L, platelets 113×10^9/L↓. Blood tests on Day +181 were: immunoglobulin G4 0.05 g/L. Nine-item common respiratory pathogen panel: negative. Antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA antibody, anti-nucleosome antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, ANCA, anti-CCP antibody, anti-streptolysin O, rheumatoid factor, and high-sensitivity CRP were negative. Bronchoscopy on Day +182 showed no neoplasm. Pathology report on Day +182 showed: (bronchoscopic biopsy of lesion in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe) submitted biopsy tissue demonstrated widened alveolar septa, collagen fiber tissue proliferation, and a small amount of lymphocytic infiltration in the interstitium, consistent with chronic inflammatory changes. The exfoliative cytology report on the 11th showed: (bronchoscopic brushing of the posterior segment of the right upper lobe) no definite malignant tumor cells seen at present. High-throughput sequencing of BALF from the "medial segment of the right middle lobe" on Day -182 showed: bacteria: Acinetobacter (Reads=2478), Escherichia coli (Reads=932), Staphylococcus aureus (Reads=800), Pseudomonas (Reads=500), Corynebacterium xerosis (Reads=153), Enterococcus faecalis (Reads=52), Alcaligenes faecalis (Reads=43). On Day -117, chest CT at a local hospital showed multiple nodules in both lungs, somewhat absorbed compared with Day +171; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes; a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs; splenomegaly; and a dense shadow in the liver. On Day -73, chest CT at a local hospital showed multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs, of undetermined nature, with lesions similar to those on Day -117; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes. On Day -6, CBC at a local hospital showed: WBC 3.05×10^9/L↓, neutrophils% 62.60%, lymphocytes% 26.60%, monocytes% 7.20%, eosinophils% 3.30%, basophils% 0.3%, neutrophils 1.91×10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.81×10^9/L↓, monocytes 0.22×10^9/L, eosinophils 0.10×10^9/L, basophils 0.01×10^9/L, RBC 4.27×10^12/L↓, hemoglobin 112 g/L↓, platelets 81×10^9/L↓. On the same day, chest CT showed multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs, of undetermined nature, with increased number and size of lesions compared with the Day -73 imaging; small mediastinal and bilateral axillary lymph nodes; and a small amount of focal inflammation in both lungs.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary lymphoproliferative disease/pulmonary lymphoma (e.g., pulmonary MALT lymphoma, pulmonary involvement by lymphoma, lymphomatoid granulomatosis)
supporting_evidence: Repeated chest CT scans showed multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs. On Day -6, compared with Day -73, the lesions had increased in number and size. Contrast-enhanced CT on Day -4 still showed multiple nodules in both lungs, representing a persistent, prolonged, and progressive imaging course.
Accompanied by mediastinal lymphadenopathy/small lymph nodes and small bilateral axillary lymph nodes
Splenomegaly is present, suggesting possible involvement of the extrathoracic lymphoreticular endothelial system.
The complete blood count showed leukopenia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia, with mild anemia developing later, suggesting a possible underlying systemic hematologic/lymphoproliferative disorder.
In approximately 3 months before Day 0, herpes zoster occurred; together with lymphopenia, this suggests abnormal cellular immune status, which may be seen in lymphatic system diseases.

Bronchoscopy showed no neoplasm, and brush cytology showed no definite malignant tumor cells; a lymphoproliferative lesion predominantly involving the pulmonary interstitium/perivascular regions, which is prone to be missed by bronchoscopic sampling, cannot be excluded.
opposing_evidence: TBLB pathology from the posterior segment of the right upper lobe showed only chronic inflammatory changes, with no definite malignant tumor cells identified
The lesions showed some absorption on Day -117 compared with Day +171, with a certain degree of fluctuation, and did not show a typical pattern of continuous unidirectional progression.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary fungal infection (such as cryptococcosis, aspergillus infection, etc.)
supporting_evidence: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with flocculent opacities; this imaging appearance can be seen in pulmonary fungal infection

The disease course has been protracted for more than half a year; the lesions previously partially resolved and then progressed again, consistent with the fluctuating characteristics of some chronic fungal infections.
The patient previously had herpes zoster and had lymphopenia and leukopenia, suggesting possible impaired immune function and an increased risk of opportunistic infection.
When bronchoscopic biopsy shows only chronic inflammatory changes and no other etiology can be identified, infectious granuloma/fungal infection should still be considered.
Cough and sputum production developed after catching a cold in October, suggesting that inflammatory activity in the lungs may have worsened.
opposing_evidence: In phase 1, BALF high-throughput sequencing did not report any fungal-related pathogens.
The patient had no prolonged systemic infectious or toxic manifestations such as fever, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or weight loss.
TBLB pathology did not indicate fungal infection or granulomatous inflammation

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
supporting_evidence: Multiple nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs; the disease course is relatively long with increased number and enlargement, and mycobacterial infection can present as multiple nodular lesions.
Accompanied by small mediastinal lymph nodes/lymphadenopathy, consistent with infectious disease and possibly accompanied by reactive lymph node changes
Lymphopenia and a history of herpes zoster are present, suggesting an increased risk of mycobacterial infection in the setting of impaired cellular immunity.
Bronchoscopy showed no neoplasm; pathology indicated only chronic inflammation, and infectious granuloma cannot yet be excluded due to possible missed diagnosis caused by sampling limitations.
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, TB toxic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss were not described, and there was no significant change in body weight.
BALF high-throughput sequencing did not report Mycobacterium tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacteria
TBLB pathology did not indicate caseous necrosis or granulomas

differential_diagnoses.name: Inflammatory pulmonary lesion/organizing pneumonia (including inflammatory nodules and nonspecific chronic inflammation)
supporting_evidence: Bronchoscopic biopsy pathology from the posterior segment of the right upper lobe showed widened alveolar septa, collagenous fibrous tissue proliferation, and a small amount of lymphocytic infiltration in the interstitium, consistent with chronic inflammatory changes.

In addition to multiple nodules, chest CT also shows flocculent opacities and a small amount of localized inflammation; on imaging, these may overlap with organizing pneumonia or inflammatory nodules.
Repeat CT on Day -117 showed absorption compared with Day +171, suggesting that some lesions have reversible inflammatory features.

After catching a chill in October, the patient developed cough and sputum production; subsequently, CT on Day -6 showed that the lesions had increased in number and size, supporting the possibility of imaging worsening following inflammatory activity.
Bronchoscopy showed no neoplasm.
opposing_evidence: The lesions persisted for more than half a year and ultimately became more numerous and larger than before; nonspecific inflammation alone cannot fully explain this.
Small lymph nodes in the mediastinum and bilateral axillae, splenomegaly, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia are not readily explained solely by organizing pneumonia.

differential_diagnoses.name: Multiple pulmonary metastases / metastatic malignant neoplasm in the lung
supporting_evidence: Imaging showed multiple nodules in both lungs, and on Day -6, compared with Day -73, the lesions were increased in number and enlarged; hematogenous metastatic tumor dissemination should be suspected.
Accompanied by mediastinal lymphadenopathy, malignant tumors may be associated with mediastinal lymph node involvement
Negative TBLB and brushings cannot completely exclude a peripheral malignancy or a malignant lesion not reached by sampling.
opposing_evidence: The patient is 37 years old, has no smoking history, and no clear clues to a primary tumor were provided in the first stage.
The lesions had previously shown some absorption compared with before; the fluctuating changes are atypical in support of metastatic tumors.
Bronchoscopy revealed no neoplasm; brush cytology showed no definite malignant tumor cells, and biopsy also showed no evidence of malignancy.
The patient is generally in good condition, with no significant change in body weight.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sarcoidosis
supporting_evidence: The patient is a 37-year-old woman. Imaging shows multiple nodules in both lungs, accompanied by small lymph nodes in the mediastinum and bilateral axillae.
Splenomegaly can be seen in systemic granulomatous diseases

When multiple autoimmune-related antibodies are negative, making pulmonary involvement associated with some connective tissue diseases relatively less supported, sarcoidosis may be considered in the differential diagnosis of granulomatous diseases.
opposing_evidence: TBLB pathology did not indicate noncaseating granulomas
Chest CT was characterized mainly by multiple nodules and flocculent opacities; in the first stage, no information on typical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy was provided.
The presence of leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and a history of herpes zoster further suggests immune abnormalities or a hematologic disorder, which sarcoidosis cannot adequately explain.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious diseases (such as pulmonary cryptococcosis, pulmonary TB, etc.)
evidence: May present as multiple nodular lesions in both lungs; the disease course may be relatively prolonged, with an insidious onset and slow progression

differential_diagnoses.name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
evidence: It can involve multiple organ systems. Fever and other symptoms are common at disease onset. In most patients, the upper respiratory tract is affected first; the lungs and kidneys are most commonly involved. Chest imaging findings are diverse, with bilateral pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation being the most typical.

differential_diagnoses.name: Sarcoidosis
evidence: Sarcoidosis is a systemic disease in which the lungs, lymph nodes, skin, and other organs may be involved. It often presents with multiple symmetric enlarged bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes without fusion, and may be accompanied by reticular, nodular, or patchy opacities in the lungs. During the active progressive stage of the disease, systemic manifestations such as fever and weight loss may occur. Blood tests may show an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated blood calcium, and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (sACE).

recommended_exams.exam: Repeat complete blood count, liver function tests, and LDH
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further laboratory testing was completed: absolute lymphocyte count persistently decreased, platelet count decreased, globulin markedly decreased, IgG4 significantly decreased, fungal D-glucan test elevated
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The course of multiple pulmonary nodules has lasted for more than 6 months. Recent imaging shows progressive increase in the number and size of the lesions, and cough and sputum production developed after October, suggesting that the disease is in an active and progressive stage. At the same time, peripheral blood repeatedly showed leukopenia, lymphopenia, and thrombocytopenia, with mild anemia later in the course. Biochemical testing showed decreased total protein and globulin and elevated LDH, and there is also a prior history of severe herpes zoster and splenomegaly, suggesting that in addition to simple focal pulmonary inflammation, there may also be an underlying immunodeficiency state, persistent infection, or systemic disease. The purpose of completing laboratory tests is to systematically assess inflammatory activity, the degree of cytopenias, organ involvement, and hypogammaglobulinemia, determine disease severity, distinguish infectious from noninfectious causes, and provide a basis for whether further invasive testing is needed, whether anti-infective therapy can be continued, or whether immunologic evaluation is required.

The patient has had multiple pulmonary nodules and flocculent opacities in both lungs for half a year, with progressive increase in number and size. In the context of persistent lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and a prior history of herpes zoster, this suggests an increased risk of opportunistic infection. Fungal D-glucan is now elevated, but prior BALF metagenomic next-generation sequencing did not detect fungi, and sputum fungal smear and culture were also negative. Therefore, this indicator needs to be rechecked and followed dynamically to determine whether there is evidence of deep fungal infection, so as to avoid misclassifying the persistently progressive pulmonary lesions as simple bacterial infection or noninfectious nodules. This test primarily addresses the key differential question of whether invasive or chronic fungal infection is present, and, together with imaging changes, etiologic results, and treatment response, can determine whether further mycologic testing or adjustment of the anti-infective strategy is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immune function testing: tendency toward hypogammaglobulinemia, abnormal T-lymphocyte subsets, decreased NK cell count
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This case not only has clues of recurrent pulmonary infection, but also has herpes zoster in approximately 3 months before Day 0, persistent lymphopenia, markedly decreased globulin, markedly decreased IgG4, and splenomegaly; these findings suggest that the patient may have combined abnormalities of humoral and cellular immunity. Multiple pulmonary nodules with detection of various opportunistic pathogens, together with symptomatic improvement after anti-infective therapy, also support susceptibility to infection in the setting of impaired immune defense. Ordering immune function testing is intended to determine whether hypogammaglobulinemia or another immunodeficiency state is present, to explain why multiple pathogens were detected, why the lesions have shown a protracted fluctuating course, and why herpes zoster and other manifestations occurred, while also helping distinguish primary or secondary immune abnormalities from simple infection, tumor, or granulomatous disease. This result will directly affect subsequent etiologic assessment, infection risk evaluation, and whether further immunology specialist evaluation and treatment strategy selection are needed.

Repeated complete blood counts in the patient showed a persistent decrease in the absolute lymphocyte count, and the patient had previously developed relatively severe herpes zoster, suggesting possible impairment of cellular immunity; the pulmonary lesions were also characterized by multiple nodules with prolonged persistence and progression, and both infectious and noninfectious etiologies need to be assessed in the context of the immune background. T-lymphocyte subset testing is helpful to determine whether the cellular immune components, including CD3, CD4, and CD8, are abnormal, and to clarify whether the patient has a predominantly T-cell immunodeficiency, thereby explaining the increased risk of opportunistic infections, the complex pathogen spectrum, and the recurrent course of illness. This test is of important value for differentiating a state of susceptibility to infection, assessing disease severity, and determining whether subsequent expansion of etiologic pathogen screening and cautious use of immunosuppressive therapy are needed.

The patient’s prior history of herpes zoster suggests possible abnormalities in antiviral and cell-mediated immune defense. In addition, the current prolonged progression of pulmonary lesions, with detection of multiple opportunistic pathogens and persistent lymphopenia, cannot be fully explained by bacterial infection alone as the cause of this susceptibility. NK cell count testing can further evaluate whether innate immunity and antiviral- and antitumor-related immune function are impaired, and clarify the scope and degree of the immune abnormality. This test is intended to determine whether the patient has a broader decline in immune surveillance function, thereby leading to recurrent infections, persistent unresolved lesions, and imaging progression; the results will help with an overall assessment of the credibility of subsequent etiologic interpretations, infection risk stratification, and the monitoring priorities during treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Imaging examination: progressively increasing number and size of multiple nodules in both lungs, mediastinal lymphadenopathy
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Since approximately 7 months before Day 0, the patient was found to have multiple nodules in both lungs. During this period, there was transient partial absorption, but around November they again showed a marked increase in number and size, accompanied by mediastinal lymphadenopathy, suggesting that the lesions were not stable benign nodules but rather an ongoing active intrapulmonary process. The patient currently also has cough and sputum production, abnormal immune function, and detection of multiple pathogens. The significance of repeat imaging lies in dynamically assessing changes in the distribution, number, size, and morphology of the lesions; determining whether the lesions improve in parallel after anti-infective treatment; and distinguishing inflammatory or infectious nodules from other noninfectious diseases. Imaging can also help assess systemic involvement such as mediastinal lymph nodes and splenomegaly, identify more representative lesions and subsequent sampling sites, and evaluate whether there is information related to the risk of invasive procedures.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Etiologic testing: BALF high-throughput sequencing detected multiple opportunistic pathogenic bacteria such as Acinetobacter, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus; sputum culture detected Staphylococcus aureus
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After a prolonged course of multiple pulmonary nodules, the patient developed cough and sputum production 10 months later, and the symptoms improved significantly after treatment with ceftazidime and linezolid, indicating that infectious factors at least contributed to the current clinical presentation. Previous BALF high-throughput sequencing detected multiple opportunistic pathogens, and subsequent sputum culture detected Staphylococcus aureus, but these results must be interpreted in the context of the underlying immune abnormality, imaging progression, and specimen source to determine whether they represent pathogens, colonizing organisms, or contamination. The purpose of continuing to complete microbiologic testing is to identify, as much as possible, the infectious pathogen responsible for the current active pulmonary lesions, to exclude missed fungi, mycobacteria, and others, to guide precise anti-infective therapy, and to avoid misinterpreting infection-related imaging findings as tumor or immune-mediated disease. Microbiologic results are crucial for confirming infection, excluding differential diagnoses, and selecting an anti-infective regimen.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: BALF high-throughput sequencing detected multiple opportunistic pathogens, including Acinetobacter, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's pulmonary lesions consisted of multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules with progressive changes. Routine bronchoscopic biopsy showed only chronic inflammation, and no definitive histologic diagnosis had previously been obtained. The patient also had lymphocytopenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, and a history of herpes zoster, suggesting an increased risk of opportunistic infection and mixed infection. In this context, BALF high-throughput sequencing can broadly detect pathogens in the lower respiratory tract and is particularly useful as a complement when conventional cultures may be negative or the pathogens are complex. The main question addressed by this test is whether the progressive multiple pulmonary nodules in an immunocompromised host are caused by occult infection or involvement of multiple pathogens, and it helps explain why prior routine pathology failed to identify a definite etiology. The results can be interpreted together with symptom improvement, sputum culture, and mycologic markers to guide whether treatment should be adjusted to target Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, or other opportunistic pathogens.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Sputum culture positive for Staphylococcus aureus
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient recently had significant cough and sputum production, with a large amount of sputum that was easy to expectorate, indicating that a lower respiratory tract secretion specimen was suitable for submission for testing; meanwhile, BALF high-throughput sequencing had previously detected pathogenic organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, and subsequent sputum culture again detected Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibility results available, and symptoms improved after anti-infective treatment, which increased its clinical relevance. The purpose of continuing sputum culture is to confirm, using a more routine and repeatable method, whether there is a cultivable bacterial infection, assess pathogen concordance and dynamic changes, distinguish persistent infection, transient colonization, or contamination, and guide subsequent antibiotic selection in combination with drug susceptibility. In this case, sputum culture helps explain the current respiratory symptoms, support the involvement of infection in disease exacerbation, and provide a basis for treatment optimization and efficacy evaluation.
